These read as a promotion rather than release notes: they don’t say what changed in the app. If they’re for the App Store, Apple describes “What’s New” as a place for version changes such as features, improvements, and fixes. The website subscription call to action may also need a policy review for the storefronts where the app is available. [Apple’s field guidance](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/reference/app-information/platform-version-information), [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/uk/)

I’d replace the sentence with the actual change in this release, such as: “Improved sign-up and fixed issues with account creation.” Use that only if those changes were made.

No. **“Live sports intel for every game” is 32 characters**, and Apple limits App Store subtitles to **30 characters**. [Apple’s subtitle guidance](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/product-page/)

**“Live sports intel, every game”** keeps the meaning and fits at **29 characters**.

Yes, **likely**. It’s 59 characters, within Apple’s 170-character promotional text limit. Make sure the app offers playoff alerts and insights, and that “sharper” and “faster” accurately describe them; Apple requires promotional metadata to reflect the app’s experience. “Playoff season is here” should also be current for your audience. [Apple’s promotional text guidance](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/product-page/), [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/)

If you can’t substantiate the improvement claims, use: **“Playoff season is here: get game alerts and insights.”**
